hero.title: The Electrical Transformer
hero.lead: 4-9 The Electrical Transformer: 4-9-1 Types of transformers · 4-9-2 Transformer laws · 4-9-3 Electrical power transmission

objectives: States the working principle of the electrical transformer and its main parts.
Distinguishes between a step-up transformer and a step-down transformer.
Writes the transformer laws and calculates its efficiency.
Explains the method used to transmit electrical power over long distances.

content.label: 📌 4-9 The Electrical Transformer
content.html: The electrical transformer is an AC device used to step up or step down an alternating voltage. Its working principle: the operation of the electrical transformer relies on the principle of mutual induction between two adjacent coils with complete magnetic coupling between them.

content.svgAriaLabel: Illustration of an electrical transformer with two coils and an iron core
content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Interactive Simulation: Parts of the Electrical Transformer (Figure 4-18)
content.descriptionHtml: An electrical transformer is made up of a closed iron core, and two electrically-insulated coils with a different number of turns: the primary coil is connected to the source, and the secondary coil is connected to the load (the device).

content.heading: 📋 The Transformer Is Made Up of the Following Parts
items: The core: made in a closed shape so that complete magnetic coupling is available in its windings, with high permeability, and made of wrought iron to reduce hysteresis losses, which increases its efficiency; it is also made in the form of thin, pressed sheets that are electrically insulated from each other to reduce eddy current losses.

Two coils, electrically insulated from each other and with a different number of turns; the primary coil is connected to the alternating source, and the secondary coil is connected to the device (the load), as shown in Figure 4-18. The transformer contains no automatic switch, so it is considered an AC device only.

content.html: In high-frequency transformers, the core is made of ferrite, which has a relatively high resistance, reducing hysteresis losses, and also has a very high magnetic permeability.

content.label: 📌 4-9-1 Types of Transformers
content.html: 1- Step-up transformers: these are transformers that raise the alternating voltage and lower the current in the secondary coil compared to the primary coil, which happens when the number of turns of the secondary coil is greater than the number of turns of the primary coil, as in the transformers connected at electrical power generating stations.

content.label: 📌 Step-down Transformers
content.html: 2- Step-down transformers: these are transformers that lower the voltage and raise the current in the secondary coil compared to the primary coil, which happens when the number of turns of the secondary coil is fewer than the number of turns of the primary coil, as in a mobile phone charger and others.

content.svgAriaLabel: Visual comparison between a step-up and step-down transformer based on the turns ratio
content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Interactive Simulation: Step-up or Step-down Transformer?
content.descriptionHtml: Move the turns-ratio slider \((N_2/N_1)\) and watch the transformer type change, alongside a schematic diagram comparing the thickness of the two coils (representing the number of turns).

labels.statusStepUpSuffix: → step-up transformer (V rises, I drops in the secondary coil)
labels.statusStepDownSuffix: → step-down transformer (V drops, I rises in the secondary coil)
labels.statusEqual: N2/N1 = 1 → equal number of turns (no step-up or step-down)

content.label: 📌 4-9-2 Transformer Laws
content.html: The ratio between the number of turns of the secondary coil and the number of turns of the primary coil is known as the turns ratio, denoted \(N_2/N_1\). If \(N_2/N_1>1\) then the transformer is a step-up transformer, and if \(N_2/N_1<1\) then the transformer is a step-down transformer. Likewise:

$$ \dfrac{N_2}{N_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{V_1} $$

where \(V_2\) represents the voltage of the secondary coil, and \(V_1\) the voltage of the primary coil.

$$ P_1 = V_1 I_1 $$

Power of the primary coil

$$ P_2 = V_2 I_2 $$

Power of the secondary coil

When the transformer is ideal, meaning its efficiency is 100%, then:

$$ P_1 = P_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad V_1 I_1 = V_2 I_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = \dfrac{I_1}{I_2} $$

This ratio applies only when the transformer is ideal.

Transformer efficiency = (power of the secondary coil ÷ power of the primary coil) × 100%

$$ \eta = \dfrac{P_2}{P_1} \times 100\% $$

where (η) represents the efficiency of the transformer.

content.heading: 📋 The Efficiency of a Transformer Does Not Reach 100% for the Following Reasons
items: Part of the electrical energy is lost as heat in the wires of the two coils.
Part of the electrical energy is lost as heat generated in the transformer's core due to eddy currents.
Part of the electrical energy is lost as hysteresis in the iron core material.

content.html: High-power transformers are immersed in a special kind of oil, because the oil acts as a radiator for the heat generated in the transformer's coils and works to cool it, thereby preserving its integrity.

content.problemHtml: A transformer has a turns ratio of \(\left(\dfrac{12}{1}\right)\) and an efficiency of 96%. If the current in the secondary coil is \((4\ \text{A})\) and the voltage of the secondary coil is \((4800\ \text{V})\), find: 1- The power of the primary coil. 2- The current of the primary coil.

content.html: What other measures can reduce power losses in transformers?

content.label: 📌 4-9-3 Electrical Power Transmission
content.html: If electrical power is sent over long distances, there will be a loss in the form of heat due to the resistance of the transmission wires, since (heat ∝ the square of the current × resistance, according to Joule's law). To reduce this lost power, electrical energy is transmitted at high voltage and low current through transmission wires carried on tall towers, using step-up transformers at the power generating station and step-down transformers supplying the load.

questions.question: The operation of the electrical transformer relies on the principle of:
options: Mutual induction between two adjacent coils
questions.explain: The operation of the electrical transformer relies on the principle of mutual induction between two adjacent coils with complete magnetic coupling between them.

questions.question: If \(N_2/N_1>1\), then the transformer is:
questions.explain: If \(N_2/N_1>1\) (the secondary coil has more turns), then the transformer steps up the voltage.

questions.question: The electrical transformer contains no automatic switch, therefore it is:
options: Works equally well with both currents
Does not work with any type of current
questions.explain: The transformer contains no automatic switch, so it is considered an AC device only.

questions.question: The total losses of a transformer do not include:
options: Heat in the wires of the two coils
Heat due to eddy currents in the core
Hysteresis losses in the iron core material
Losses resulting from connecting the transformer to a DC source
questions.explain: The three main transformer losses are: heat in the coil wires, heat from eddy currents in the core, and hysteresis losses in the core material — and a transformer is never connected to a DC source in the first place.

questions.question: To reduce the power lost when transmitting electrical energy over long distances, the power is sent as:
options: Both high voltage and high current
Both low voltage and low current
questions.explain: Electrical energy is transmitted at high voltage and low current to reduce power lost as heat (per Joule's law: heat ∝ the square of the current), using step-up transformers at generation and step-down transformers at the load.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: The transformer works on the principle of mutual induction between two coils on a closed iron core; it is an AC device only.
For an ideal transformer: \(V_2/V_1=I_1/I_2\); efficiency \(\eta=(P_2/P_1)\times100\%\), which never reaches 100% due to heat, eddy-current, and hysteresis losses.
Power transmission uses high voltage and low current to reduce heat loss, with step-up transformers at generation and step-down transformers at the load.
